shows.title: Seascapes Enoura | Pre-Photography Time-Recording Device
shows.description:
Hiroshi Sugimoto has been photographing the sea, in black and white, from every ocean he can reach, for more than four decades, and the results always look identical at first glance: a horizon line splitting the frame exactly in half, water below, sky above, no land, no boats, no people. This show revisits the Seascapes series through the lens of Enoura Observatory, the sculpture-garden-slash-optical-instrument Sugimoto built into a hillside overlooking Sagami Bay, where the horizon itself becomes a kind of camera obscura aligned with the summer and winter solstices.

The "pre-photography" of the title is the point — Sugimoto is less interested in the camera as a documentary tool than as the latest in a long lineage of devices humans have built to fix time and light in place, from stone circles to observatories to his own optical glass stage at Enoura. Seeing the photographs alongside that architectural and conceptual framework changes how blank they seem; each identical-looking horizon becomes a very specific record of a very specific moment, watched by a very specific structure.

Gallery Koyanagi's Ginza space, itself partly designed by Sugimoto, is a fitting place to encounter this material at human scale rather than museum scale — the seascapes were always meant to be looked at slowly, and a commercial gallery's quiet is closer to their spirit than a crowded retrospective would be.

venue.name: Gallery Koyanagi
hours: Closed Sun, Mon and national holidays

shows.title: Original Copy
shows.description:
Oriol Vilanova builds his work out of other people's discards: postcards bought by the hundreds at flea markets and secondhand stalls across Europe, sorted by motif rather than origin, and arranged into grids and constellations on gallery walls. This first Japanese solo show, guest-texted by collector and Yokohama University of Art professor Daisuke Miyazu, presents new postcard pieces made specifically for the Roppongi space, laid out with an emphasis on empty wall and negative space that nods to both Japanese design sensibility and modernist minimalism.

Each work groups anywhere from two to thirty-two identical printed postcards, objects that are mechanically reproduced on their image side but individually singular on their written, addressed reverse. That tension between mass reproduction and one-off use runs through the whole show, echoing Walter Benjamin's writing on the "aura" of the original in an age of mechanical copying. A smaller adjoining room holds a piece built around a postcard of a Monet water lily painting tucked into the pocket of an artist's work jacket, a piece that folds in the history of Impressionist brushwork alongside the history of labor clothing.

Vilanova, who trained as an architect, has spent over a decade combing flea markets for these postcards and reading spaces as sculptural problems; this show follows his large-scale postcard installation for the Spanish Pavilion at the current Venice Biennale. Original Copy is a quieter, more spare counterpart to that project — worth seeing for how much atmosphere Vilanova can wring from humble, well-traveled scraps of paper.

venue.name: Kotaro Nukaga
venue.about: KOTARO NUKAGA is a contemporary art gallery founded in Tokyo in 2018 by director Kotaro Nukaga, who also runs the historic NUKAGA GALLERY. The gallery operates three spaces in Tokyo—two in the Tennoz district (Tennoz and Three) and one in Roppongi—positioning itself at the intersection of Japanese and international contemporary practice. Its program favors avant-garde and cross-disciplinary work, drawing on history, science and technology to question established art-world discourse. The gallery represents a mix of emerging and established Japanese and overseas artists, supporting their development through exhibitions, artist liaison services and participation in international art fairs, while aiming to expand the boundaries of conventional gallery programming.

shows.title: You made me leave home...
shows.description:
Rina Banerjee builds her sculptures the way a magpie might build a nest, if the magpie had read a lot of postcolonial theory: glass chandeliers, ostrich eggs, cowrie shells, cotton thread, feathers, resin, taxidermy forms and found textiles, fused into hybrid female figures that look simultaneously ceremonial and slightly alien. Born in Kolkata and long based in New York, Banerjee trained as a polymer engineer before turning to art, and that background shows in how confidently her sculptures balance improbable, top-heavy accumulations of material.

This exhibition, drawn from the Fondation Louis Vuitton's collection, marks both the twentieth anniversary of the Espaces Louis Vuitton and the tenth anniversary of the foundation's "Hors-les-murs" program, which sends pieces from the Paris collection to satellite spaces worldwide. Alongside the sculptures are paintings that borrow visual grammar from Indian miniatures, Chinese silk painting and Aztec drawing, flattening and layering pattern in ways that echo the sculptures' own dense, accretive logic.

Banerjee's work is explicitly about migration, displacement and the residue colonialism leaves on everyday materials from "the tropical zone," as she puts it — but it delivers that critique with a lightness and visual extravagance that keeps the work from ever feeling didactic. Seeing it inside a luxury-brand exhibition space adds its own layer of friction that the artist would probably appreciate.

venue.name: Espace Louis Vuitton Tokyo
venue.about: Espace Louis Vuitton Tokyo is a non-commercial exhibition space inaugurated in 2011, occupying a glass box on the top floor of the Louis Vuitton building in Omotesando, designed by Japanese architect Jun Aoki. Rather than a gallery representing artists for sale, it functions as an art space encouraging the creation of new contemporary artworks, staging rotating exhibitions by international contemporary artists such as Yayoi Kusama and Rina Banerjee. It is linked to a sister space, Espace Louis Vuitton Osaka, and to the Fondation Louis Vuitton, reflecting Louis Vuitton's broader engagement with contemporary art. Admission is free, and the program emphasizes striking architecture as much as the art displayed within it.

shows.title: Spilling Body
shows.description:
Seiran Tsuno trained as a nurse before turning to fashion, and that dual background runs through everything in this show. Her signature works are dresses drawn in mid-air with a 3D pen — rigid, resin-lined silhouettes that trace the human form without ever accommodating it, hung from the neck like a body that has stepped out of its own outline. "Spilling Body" brings several of these garment-sculptures together with video, drawing, collage and a group of new prints made using beeswax, a material Tsuno is drawn to because it is itself a bodily excretion — fat metabolized and pushed out past the skin into something else entirely.

The exhibition's title plays on that double sense of a body that spills something and a body that is itself spilling over its own edges. Having spent years working alongside psychiatric patients and thinking about care, and having recently completed graduate research on fat embodiment under aesthetician Ito Asa, Tsuno treats dressmaking less as a way to flatter a body than as a way to keep renegotiating a relationship with a body that won't behave — pulling away from it, then reaching back toward it, over and over.

This is Tsuno's first solo show at a commercial gallery in Tokyo, arriving just months after her graduate thesis show, an exhibition at the 21st Century Museum of Contemporary Art in Kanazawa, and the acquisition of one of her dresses by the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York. It's a chance to see the sculptural dresses that built her reputation alongside newer, quieter works on paper that extend the same questions into different materials.
shows.reception: Fashion-focused dialogue viewing event on Sunday, August 23, 2026 (12:00–15:00 reserved for event participants)

venue.name: EUKARYOTE
venue.about: EUKARYOTE is a contemporary art gallery in Jingumae, Shibuya-ku, Tokyo, established in 2018. Taking its name from the biological term for organisms whose cells contain a nucleus, the gallery frames its program around a recurring cycle of artistic evolution, likening it to the metabolism of living systems. It presents artists and artworks engaging with the tension between tangibility and intangibility in contemporary practice. Since opening, EUKARYOTE has regularly participated in art fairs across Japan and abroad, including ART OSAKA, Art Fair Asia Fukuoka, Art Collaboration Kyoto, and international fairs such as ART OnO Seoul, alongside group exhibitions and gallery-weekend events in Tokyo. The gallery represents a roster of primarily Japanese contemporary artists working across painting and other media.

shows.title: Original Copy
shows.description:
Oriol Vilanova's first solo show in Japan builds an installation entirely out of postcards — mass-produced, secondhand, gathered over years from flea markets and junk shops around the world. The Barcelona-based artist, who trained as an architect, arranges these small printed images against the gallery's walls with a restraint that plays off the surrounding space itself; the works range from pairs of near-identical cards to groupings of up to thirty-two copies of the same image, turning repetition into a kind of quiet arithmetic.

Vilanova showed a related, much larger version of this postcard-based practice earlier in 2026 at the Spanish Pavilion of the Venice Biennale, where postcards blanketed the interior like a mosaic. Here the approach is inverted: negative space and the architecture of the Roppongi gallery itself become part of the composition. A smaller room holds Old Masters (Monet), built around a postcard of a Monet painting tucked into the pocket of the well-worn work jacket Vilanova wears while scouring markets — a piece that folds art history, labor, and the postcard's own status as souvenir into one image.

What makes the show worth seeing is the tension built into its title: postcards are the ultimate cheap copy, printed by the thousands and passed hand to hand, yet each one that was actually mailed carries a unique message and history on its reverse. Vilanova's quiet, spare installations ask what's left of an image's authenticity once it's been endlessly reproduced and endlessly personalized at the same time.

shows.title: Medicine Infrastructure via Map — Tomoko Konoike's Summer School
shows.description:
Tomoko Konoike turns the Ryogoku gallery into a functioning schoolhouse for the run of this show, mapping out the wide-ranging, semi-nomadic practice she has built since her 2020 solo presentation at the Artizon Museum. Rather than a conventional survey of finished objects, the exhibition assembles architectural drawings, archival material, and works in progress alongside documentation of her ongoing off-site projects — including the loan of sculptures to shops, gardens and shrines around Japan as "temporary repositories," and the touring "Wolf Bench" pieces that traveled on from Expo 2025 Osaka.

The gallery hosts a running program of guest lectures, readings and craft sessions timed to the show, with visiting speakers spanning sculpture, folklore studies, game design and architecture — an unusual structure that treats the exhibition as pedagogy in progress rather than a fixed hang. New works made specifically for this run appear alongside the archival and process material, so the space functions as both retrospective and open studio.

Konoike has spent recent years responding to disruption — the pandemic, the Noto Peninsula earthquake, an Osaka Expo — by decentralizing how and where her art lives, and this show is the clearest single articulation of that impulse: a "summer school" that asks what it means to keep an artist's work circulating through everyday life rather than warehousing it.

venue.name: GALLERY MoMo Ryogoku
venue.about: GALLERY MoMo is a contemporary art gallery in Tokyo, established in 2003 in Roppongi. In 2008 it opened a larger space in Ryogoku, and in 2013 the original Roppongi space was reopened as GALLERY MoMo Projects, focused on discovering young Japanese and international artists and curators. The gallery mainly represents Japanese artists born in the 1970s and 1980s, whose work reflects contemporary states of mind through personal styles, while also seeking connections to a global artistic context. Its stated mission is to introduce international artists with distinctive concepts to Japanese audiences, and to bring Japanese artists to audiences abroad.

shows.title: Yoshio Sekine: From the "Gate" and "Boxcar" Series
shows.description:
Yoshio Sekine (1922–1989) was a founding member of the Gutai group who broke from its material experiments to spend decades painting the same handful of motifs — abacuses, level-crossing gates, and boxcars — over and over from a flattened, frontal or side-on viewpoint that refuses conventional perspective. This exhibition gathers works from the gate and boxcar series he developed alongside his better-known abacus paintings between the 1960s and mid-1970s, along with earlier experimental pieces, tracing how a single, almost diagrammatic vocabulary hardened into one of postwar Japan's most idiosyncratic bodies of abstract-figurative painting.

What's striking in the works on view is how industrial infrastructure — a railway gate, a line of freight cars — gets treated with the same cool, blueprint-like detachment Sekine brought to his abacus beads: flattened silhouettes, repeated modular units, and a refusal of illusionistic depth. The effect sits somewhere between technical drawing and hard-edge abstraction, and it's easy to see why critics have linked this phase of his career to his broader anti-illusionist project.

For a gallery that has represented Sekine's estate for decades, this is a chance to see a lesser-exhibited corner of his practice — the gate and boxcar paintings rarely travel as a dedicated group — alongside the abacus works that made his reputation, filling out the picture of an artist who kept circling back to the same few images to strip painting down to its structural bones.

venue.name: Tokyo Gallery + BTAP
venue.about: Tokyo Gallery + BTAP is Japan's oldest contemporary art gallery, founded in Tokyo in 1950 by Yamamoto Takashi together with Shimizu Kusuo, initially as the Sukiyabashi Gallery. From the late 1950s it introduced Western abstraction, Gutai, Neo Dada and Mono-ha artists, later becoming a key champion of postwar Korean and Chinese contemporary art. In 2002 it opened BTAP in Beijing's 798 Art Zone, and in 2006 adopted its current dual name. Led today by Yamamoto Toyotsugu in Tokyo and Tabata Yukito in Beijing, the gallery continues to present postwar Japanese art alongside younger generations of artists across Japan, Korea and China, and takes part regularly in international art fairs.

shows.title: As One Draws: TSCA 20th Anniversary Group Exhibition
shows.description:
To mark two decades in business, Takuro Someya Contemporary Art has pulled together sixteen artists from across its history into a single group show — a rare chance to see the gallery's roster side by side rather than in the usual sequence of solo exhibitions. The title, "As One Draws," points to drawing and mark-making as a loose connective thread, though the artists range widely in medium: painting, photography, sculpture, digital and generative work, and installation.

The lineup mixes long-associated names like Kenjiro Okazaki, Rafaël Rozendaal, Enrico Isamu Oyama, and Goro Murayama — artists who have each anchored solo shows here over the years — with photographers and sculptors such as Mayumi Hosokura, Shuhei Ise, and the duo Mai Yamashita + Naoto Kobayashi. Harm van den Dorpel's algorithmically generated pieces sit alongside more traditionally hand-worked drawings and paintings by Chinoko Sakamoto, Hideki Makiguchi, and Kaai Tsuji, giving a sense of just how broad the gallery's definition of "drawing" has become.

As an anniversary survey, the show works less as a themed argument and more as a group portrait of a gallery's history — useful for anyone trying to get a quick overview of who TSCA has championed since it opened, and a good complement to the concurrent photography-focused show upstairs in the same space.

venue.name: Takuro Someya Contemporary Art
hours: Closed Sun, Mon and National Holidays
venue.about: Takuro Someya Contemporary Art (TSCA) is a contemporary art gallery in Tokyo's Higashi-Shinagawa district, housed within the Terrada Art Complex. The gallery represents a small roster of Japanese and international artists working across painting, sculpture, photography, video and net-based media, including figures such as Kenjiro Okazaki, Rafaël Rozendaal, Mayumi Hosokura and Masaru Iwai. TSCA regularly mounts solo and group exhibitions in its Tokyo space and participates in major international art fairs, presenting its artists' work in dialogue with wider contemporary art discourse. The program spans generations, from established figures with museum retrospectives to younger practitioners exploring digital and performative practices.

shows.title: Night Ruins
shows.description:
British painter Nigel Cooke's Pace Tokyo debut gathers a body of new paintings built around ruined, moonlit landscapes — crumbling architecture, tangled vegetation and isolated figures rendered in the thick, sedimentary layers of paint that have become his signature. Cooke has long treated the canvas as an excavation site, scraping back and rebuilding surfaces until image and material history become inseparable, and these nocturnal scenes push that process toward something closer to romantic ruin painting filtered through decades of punk and graffiti culture.

Cooke first drew attention in the early 2000s for large paintings that mashed up art-historical landscape tropes with cartoonish decay and text-based graffiti, and his practice has since matured into a more painterly, atmospheric mode without losing its interest in collapse and entropy. "Night Ruins" reads as a meditation on twilight states — between construction and decay, figuration and abstraction, control and accident.

Coming just after his presentation in the Venice Biennale's collateral program, this show offers a concentrated look at where Cooke's moody, densely worked landscapes stand right now, in one of Roppongi's most polished exhibition spaces.

venue.name: Pace Tokyo
venue.about: Pace Gallery is a global contemporary art gallery founded in Boston in 1960 by Arne Glimcher, now led by CEO Marc Glimcher and President Samanthe Rubell. Working with roughly eighty artists and several estates, Pace's program pairs emerging and established contemporary figures with twentieth-century forebears, spanning painting, sculpture, photography, and light-based installation. The gallery operates spaces in New York, Los Angeles, London, Geneva, Berlin, Seoul, and Tokyo, with offices in Beijing and Hong Kong. Its Tokyo location, in the Azabudai Hills development, presents exhibitions by artists including Nigel Cooke and forms part of Pace's growing presence across Asia.

shows.title: Special Feature Exhibition: Nobuo Yamanaka, Luisa Lambri, Mayumi Hosokura
shows.artist: Nobuo Yamanaka, Luisa Lambri, Mayumi Hosokura
shows.description:
This three-artist photography exhibition pairs a pioneer of Japanese conceptual photography with two artists working in very different registers of the medium today. Nobuo Yamanaka, who worked mostly in the 1970s, is represented here by pinhole-camera images of the sun — direct, almost diagrammatic records of light itself, made with a technique that strips photography back to its most basic optical principle. Luisa Lambri, showing in cooperation with Gallery Koyanagi, contributes cibachrome prints from her long-running studies of modernist architecture, in which apartment blocks and interiors dissolve into soft fields of light and shadow rather than legible structures.

Mayumi Hosokura's work provides the show's contemporary anchor, with large-format C-type prints from her "KAZAN" series alongside more recent pieces — images that treat volcanic and bodily forms with the same cool, saturated palette she's become known for. Seeing Yamanaka's austere solar studies next to Lambri's dissolving architecture and Hosokura's charged color photography makes for a useful conversation about how differently photographers across generations have used the camera to register light, space, and the body.

The exhibition runs concurrently with TSCA's twentieth-anniversary group show "As One Draws," making this a good moment to see the gallery's program in some depth.

venue.name: Takuro Someya Contemporary Art
hours: Closed Sun, Mon and National Holidays
venue.about: Takuro Someya Contemporary Art (TSCA) is a contemporary art gallery in Tokyo's Higashi-Shinagawa district, housed within the Terrada Art Complex. The gallery represents a small roster of Japanese and international artists working across painting, sculpture, photography, video and net-based media, including figures such as Kenjiro Okazaki, Rafaël Rozendaal, Mayumi Hosokura and Masaru Iwai. TSCA regularly mounts solo and group exhibitions in its Tokyo space and participates in major international art fairs, presenting its artists' work in dialogue with wider contemporary art discourse. The program spans generations, from established figures with museum retrospectives to younger practitioners exploring digital and performative practices.

shows.title: Man Ray
shows.description:
Take Ninagawa devotes its main space to Man Ray, running photography, painting, and object-based sculpture side by side to make the point that the artist's restless experimentation wasn't confined to the darkroom. Man Ray treated chess as more than a pastime — he was a serious, lifelong player and designed his own surrealist chess sets — and the game recurs here as both subject and structural metaphor, a system of logic, chance, and strategy that runs parallel to how he approached picture-making itself.

Seeing rayographs, canvases, and sculptural objects together underscores how consistently Man Ray dismantled the boundaries between mediums; an object photographed, painted, and cast could all be treated as versions of a single idea. The show is timed alongside recent international reappraisals of his work, including the Metropolitan Museum's 2025–26 rayograph survey, and offers a rare chance to see this range of his output in Tokyo.

The gallery has paired the exhibition with a concurrent, adjacent presentation of On Kawara, drawing out an unexpected kinship between two very different artists who both used serial, repeated gestures to register the passage of time — well worth seeing as a single visit across both rooms.

shows.title: On Kawara: I Got Up
shows.description:
This is a focused selection from one of On Kawara's defining conceptual projects: I Got Up, a twelve-year series of postcards the artist mailed daily to friends, family, collectors, and colleagues between 1968 and 1979, each rubber-stamped with the exact time he rose that morning and the date and place of sending. It's one of several serial, date-based projects — alongside his better-known Date Paintings — through which Kawara turned the most mundane fact of daily existence into an obsessively documented, decades-long record.

The postcards on view include ones addressed to figures such as William Copley, the artist and dealer closely tied to the Surrealist circle around Man Ray, whose concurrent exhibition occupies the gallery's other space. That pairing is the point: Kawara's postcards trace a line from his early Surrealist-inflected figuration toward the rigorously systemic conceptual art he's now known for, and seeing the work next to Man Ray highlights two very different strategies — one embracing chance and invention, the other repetition and system — for using art to register the passage of time.

For anyone who knows Kawara mainly through the stark black Date Paintings, I Got Up is a warmer, more intimate entry point: real names, real destinations, the small bureaucratic ritual of stamping a card repeated single day after single day for over a decade.

shows.title: Artists Discovered Through Social Media — Then, Now, and the Future
shows.artist: Emi Kuraya, Utanhole, MADSAKI, Momoka Ota, Hideyasu Moto, Kuru Yumeno, Naoki Saito, Mai Kurotaki, Hideki Maekawa, YEYE, Isoo Togawa, Alison Friend
shows.description:
This group show is Kaikai Kiki Gallery's own case study in how the art market has changed since Instagram became a viable discovery channel for young artists. The premise, laid out by Takashi Murakami himself in the gallery's statement, is straightforward: gather a dozen artists the gallery first noticed on social media over the past several years, and show both the work that got them noticed and what they're making now, as a way of taking the temperature of a gallery ecosystem that Murakami argues is currently contracting.

The roster ranges from gallery mainstays like MADSAKI and Emi Kuraya to younger names such as Utanhole, Momoka Ota, and YEYE, alongside illustrators-turned-painters like Alison Friend. Utanhole's large, unsettling figure paintings — built up in oil, acrylic gouache and colored pencil — anchor the visual identity of the show. Expect a mix of painting and illustration-adjacent work rather than a single unified aesthetic; the connecting thread is biographical (how each artist got found) rather than formal.

The exhibition runs alongside a series of ticketed talks featuring Murakami, dealer Tomio Koyama, and others discussing the state of the gallery market in 2026 — context that makes this less a conventional survey than a self-aware group portrait of a particular moment in how contemporary art gets discovered and sold.

venue.name: Kaikai Kiki Gallery
hours: Closed Sun, Mon and public holidays
venue.about: Kaikai Kiki Gallery occupies the basement of an office building in Motoazabu, Tokyo, that once served as the private viewing room for Kaikai Kiki's headquarters. The space was reopened as a public gallery in March 2008, after Kaikai Kiki relocated from a prefab studio in Saitama's Asaka city to Tokyo in 2006. The gallery presents exhibitions of its own roster of Kaikai Kiki artists alongside international figures such as Mark Grotjahn, Matthew Monahan, Seonna Hong and Friedrich Kunath, aiming to build connections between Japanese and international contemporary art. Its stated goal is to manage artists and sell work in a way that gives art new social value, continuing to invite artists from both Japan and abroad to exhibit in its roughly 197 square meter exhibition space.

shows.title: ShugoArts Show
shows.artist: Naofumi Maruyama, Ritsue Mishima, Kan Yasuda
shows.description:
Three very different sculptural and painterly languages share the gallery's rooms in this late-summer group presentation, built around new and recent work by three artists ShugoArts has represented for years. Naofumi Maruyama, one of Japan's key painters since the 1990s, contributes canvases and works on paper made with his signature staining technique — acrylic worked into water-soaked cotton so that figures and landscape dissolve into one another, hovering between representation and abstraction.

Ritsue Mishima, who has lived and worked between Venice and Kyoto since the late 1980s, shows colorless glass sculptures made in collaboration with Murano's glassblowers; her pieces are less about glass as material than about how it gathers and releases ambient light and air, which is part of why her work has moved as easily into architecture and public space as into galleries. Kan Yasuda, based in Pietrasanta, Italy since the 1970s, rounds out the show with marble and bronze sculptures — his monumental, impossibly smooth forms have been installed permanently in public sites across Europe and Japan, and here appear at gallery scale.

Putting these three together makes an interesting case: a painter dissolving form into surface, a glass artist capturing air and light in transparent volume, and a sculptor carving weight into apparent weightlessness. It's a chance to see three senior, internationally exhibited artists in dialogue rather than in solo survey, in the gallery's Roppongi space inside complex665.

shows.title: The Spirituality Embodied in Sculpture
shows.artist: Futoshi Miyagi, Yuko Mohri, Trevor Yeung, Tomoya Matsuzaki
shows.description:
This group show at Yutaka Kikutake's Roppongi space asks what sculpture can carry beyond its physical mass — the show's title points toward objects and installations that hold something closer to atmosphere, memory or ritual than pure form. Four artists with very different toolkits are brought together: Futoshi Miyagi, known for work that threads personal and queer history through Okinawa's postwar landscape; Yuko Mohri, whose kinetic, precariously balanced assemblages of found objects and everyday machinery have made her one of Japan's most internationally visible sculptors; Trevor Yeung, whose plant- and aquarium-based installations probe intimacy, care and control; and Tomoya Matsuzaki, whose sculptural practice engages more directly with material process and structure.

Seen together, the works suggest sculpture as a vessel for states that are hard to picture directly — longing, care, ecological anxiety, spiritual residue — rather than as a discipline concerned with mass and volume for their own sake. It's a chance to see Mohri's delicate mechanisms and Yeung's living, tended-to installations in direct conversation with more historically and materially grounded work by Miyagi and Matsuzaki.

The exhibition runs the length of summer into early autumn at Kikutake's Piramide building space, one of Roppongi's more research-driven programs for younger and mid-career Japanese and regional artists.

venue.name: Yutaka Kikutake Gallery
hours: Closed Sun, Mon and national holidays
venue.about: Yutaka Kikutake Gallery opened in Roppongi, Tokyo, in 2015, later adding a second space in Kyobashi in 2024. The gallery presents exhibitions of international and domestic artists, supporting their practices and seeking opportunities to present their work internationally. Grounded in a strong sense of recent art history, the program explores newly created forms of expression and emphasizes art's contribution to society. Beyond exhibitions, the gallery runs workshops for all ages and publishes artist books alongside the lifestyle and culture magazine Chic and the art criticism journal Kyoku. The Kyobashi space focuses on group exhibitions reflecting the gallery's core values.

shows.title: Chimimōryō – Here
shows.description:
Naoko Majima has spent more than fifty years making drawings and objects by working with her whole body, laying huge sheets of paper on the floor and letting physical sensation guide dense, cell-like networks of line across the surface. This exhibition, her first solo show at Mizuma in fourteen years, is built mainly around new sculpture, assembled from a personal accumulation of materials: animal bones found near Mount Fuji, penny-candy prizes, driftwood collected in France, a single bird's feathers, weaving thread left by her late mother, scraps of her own clothing, even a chair from her studio.

The title refers to "chimimōryō" — formless spirit-presences she describes not as folkloric monsters but as things she genuinely senses inhabiting wind, water, stone and forest, quietly existing alongside her through difficult periods of her life. The sculptures, built from personal remnants and cast-off materials, read as small offerings to those presences, objects poised on the edge of collapse that nonetheless carry a plainly celebratory charge.

Alongside the new work, the gallery is showing previously unseen drawings from the 1990s and a reworked koi sculpture from the same period, giving a sense of how her vocabulary of pulsing organic form has extended from paper into three dimensions over three decades. Majima's work has been the subject of major museum surveys at the Nagoya City Art Museum and Ashikaga Museum of Art, and this show offers a rare, tightly focused look at where her practice stands today.

venue.name: Mizuma Art Gallery
venue.about: Mizuma Art Gallery was founded in Tokyo in 1994 by executive director Mizuma Sueo. The gallery introduces Japanese and Asian artists with distinctive, style-independent sensibilities to the international art scene. As contemporary art markets in Asia expanded, Mizuma opened a Beijing space in 2008 and a Singapore gallery at Gillman Barracks in 2012, followed by an artist residence, Rumah Kijang Mizuma, in Yogyakarta in 2014 to foster exchange between Japanese and Indonesian artists. The gallery is known for active participation in major international fairs such as Art Basel Hong Kong and The Armory Show, and for producing artists who have gone on to international careers.

shows.title: Liminal
shows.description:
Hogalee draws women, over and over, using the clean, codified linework of manga and comics — but strips out the narrative captions and speech bubbles that usually tell you how to read them. The repetition is the method: by returning again and again to a single, deceptively simple motif, she turns a pop-cultural shorthand for femininity into something more ambiguous and harder to pin down, closer to a symbol under examination than an illustration doing a job.

"Liminal" pushes that ambiguity further, focusing on the in-between states her figures seem to inhabit — neither fully individuated portraits nor pure icons, existing somewhere between the mirror-like flatness of a printed image and the presence of an actual body. It's a fitting direction for an artist who has spent recent years moving between gallery walls and public, outdoor installations, testing how the same image behaves differently depending on where and how it's encountered.

Kana Kawanishi's Kiyosumi-Shirakawa space, a short walk from the Museum of Contemporary Art Tokyo, has built a reputation on exactly this kind of focused, image-based conceptual work, and Hogalee's exacting, line-driven paintings are a good fit for the gallery's usual register.

venue.name: Kana Kawanishi Gallery
hours: Closed Sun, Mon, Tue and national holidays
venue.about: Kana Kawanishi Gallery is a Tokyo contemporary art gallery led by director Kana Kawanishi, operating two exhibition spaces in the city: a gallery in Kiyosumi‑Shirakawa and a photography‑focused space, Kana Kawanishi Photography, in Nishi‑Azabu. The gallery represents a roster of mostly Japanese artists working across photography, painting, sculpture and mixed‑media installation, alongside a smaller group of international artists, including Finnish photographers. Its program mixes solo and group exhibitions with an active presence at international art fairs such as NADA New York, Frieze Seoul, Unseen Amsterdam, Photo London and Photo Basel, as well as Tokyo‑based fairs like Hibiya Okuroji and Art Fair Tokyo. The gallery also runs an affiliated art office handling publication, translation and editorial projects for artists and institutions.

shows.title: Lacuna or Extension
shows.description:
Keisuke Shirota builds his paintings around a photograph, then paints outward from it in monochrome, letting invented, half-remembered landscape fill the canvas beyond the photographic frame. The color image at the center of each work reads as documentary fact; the grayscale extension around it is conjecture, an imagined continuation built from what the photo implies rather than what it shows. The effect is a picture that seems to keep going past its own edges, as though memory were leaking out past the borders of a snapshot.

The show's title, "Lacuna or Extension," points to the gaps Shirota builds into these compositions — blank margins and seams between photographic and painted zones that mark the boundary between the real and the fabricated. In several works two panels mirror and swap positions, producing a looping, repeating structure rather than a single fixed image, so that the paintings feel less like discrete scenes than open-ended sequences.

Shirota, born in 1975 in Kanagawa and a graduate of Tokyo University of the Arts' graduate design program, had a solo museum show at the Chigasaki City Museum of Art in 2019–2020. His work sits at an interesting hinge point for photography now that photographs themselves are widely understood to be manipulable — asking what exactly we're looking at when the line between recorded and imagined image has blurred.

venue.name: Maki Fine Arts
venue.about: Maki Fine Arts is a contemporary art gallery in Tokyo, founded in the fall of 2010 by director Takahiro Maki. The gallery originally opened in Chuo-ku and relocated in 2015 to its current space in Kagurazaka, Shinjuku-ku. Its program represents a group of Japanese and international artists working across painting, sculpture, and mixed media, and the gallery regularly participates in art fairs in Japan and abroad, including NADA New York, Art Fair Tokyo, and Art Collaboration Kyoto. Represented artists have also been featured in institutional exhibitions at museums such as the Museum of Contemporary Art Tokyo and the National Museum of Modern Art, Tokyo.

shows.title: Painting to Communicate with Someone Unknown
shows.description:
Natsuko Sakamoto's first solo presentation with Tomio Koyama Gallery brings together a new body of large-scale oil paintings built from her signature process: interlocking cellular, tile-like grids that she completes section by section without reworking, letting the accumulated "mistakes" of the method generate warped, labyrinthine pictorial spaces. Female figures, often standing in for the artist herself, occupy these disorienting environments, caught between legibility and abstraction.

Sakamoto, who trained through a doctoral program at Aichi University of the Arts, has spent over a decade shifting her practice away from narrative painting toward an investigation of what she calls "a way of touching a space that does not yet exist." The Roppongi presentation extends that inquiry with fresh canvases that push her tile-and-figure vocabulary further into pure spatial invention.

It's a good opportunity to see an artist mid-transition — someone whose formal language of grids and glitches has been building for years in smaller Tokyo and Nagoya galleries — get a full-scale outing at one of Roppongi's most consistent painting-focused programs.

venue.name: Tomio Koyama Gallery
hours: Closed Sun, Mon and national holidays
venue.about: Tomio Koyama Gallery is a Tokyo contemporary art gallery founded in 1996 in Saga-cho, Koto-ku, by Tomio Koyama. It has since expanded to multiple spaces across the city, currently operating in Roppongi, Tennoz and Kyobashi (opened 2024), as well as a space in Maebashi. Since its founding the gallery has been active on the international art fair circuit and has served as an early platform for young Japanese artists, helping to shape a current within Japanese contemporary art. It represents artists including Kishio Suga, Mika Ninagawa, Hiroshi Sugito and Richard Tuttle, alongside ceramic artists, and presents a program spanning established and emerging talents across nationalities and media.

shows.title: BEFORE THE POINTING
shows.description:
Teru Noji built his visual language far from Tokyo's gallery system — as a graphic designer who spent his childhood shuttling between Hong Kong and the United States, then went on to live nomadically across India, Latin America, and Africa before settling in Arles in the south of France. That itinerant history shows up in the work here: familiar domestic objects, dolls, and porcelain figures are reworked with hand-designed decals applied like tattoos, and finished with cosmetic makeup that gives inert forms an unsettling, almost sentient presence.

The exhibition gathers new pieces built around Noji's ongoing interest in the moment before recognition tips into unease — the instant when something ordinary starts to feel slightly wrong. Figurines and vessels carry painted symbols and fragmentary text that read like tattoos or ritual markings, blurring the line between decorative craft and psychological portrait. Installation photographs from the gallery show a dense, cabinet-of-curiosities hang, with individual sculptural objects given room to be examined up close.

Having first returned to Japan for a show in 2022 after eighteen years abroad, Noji continues to work at the crossroads of graphic design and outsider-adjacent contemporary art, mixing humor, mild menace, and evident affection for his materials. This is a compact, object-based show best appreciated in person, where the tactile decal work and finish on each piece can actually be read.

venue.name: KOMIYAMA TOKYO G
venue.about: KOMIYAMA TOKYO G is a gallery space in Tokyo's Kanda-Jimbocho book district, launched in 2022 by the century-old secondhand bookstore Komiyama Shoten. It presents solo exhibitions and group shows spanning photography, illustration, ceramics, tattoo art, fashion and fetish culture, often mixing the bookstore's archival material with contemporary artists' work. Throughout the year it also hosts art book fairs and publication-related exhibitions tied to photobooks and artist monographs. The program favors emerging and cult-following artists working in painting, ceramics, digital/CG art, airbrush illustration, and documentary photography, reflecting the eclectic subcultural interests of its bookstore origins.

shows.title: Eiichiro Oda's ONE PIECE / The Scroll II
shows.description:
This touring presentation turns a single sprawling ONE PIECE illustration into an object built more like a temple treasure than a poster. Oda's Hundred Views of Pirates — originally drawn across three consecutive issues of Weekly Shonen Jump to mark the manga's 1000th chapter and a fan-voted "World Top 100" character poll — has been re-rendered onto handmade Echizen washi paper and printed using color collotype, a 19th-century photomechanical process kept alive by only one workshop in the world, Kyoto's Benrido. Each of the three connected sheets required 23 separate printing plates, an almost absurd level of craft for a picture of pirates.

Alongside the scroll hangs Covers, a run of ONE PIECE book-jacket illustrations printed the same way on washi and shown in Tokyo for the first time — sixteen of them installed for this run, drawn from decades of the series' cover art. Seeing Oda's linework migrate from glossy commercial paper stock to something as tactile and slow as hand-laid washi is the real hook here: familiar images gain a texture and gravity that mass printing was never built to hold.

It's a commercial gallery as much as an exhibition — prints and scrolls are for sale, at prices that place them closer to fine-art editions than manga merchandise — but the display itself, and the chance to see collotype printing used on pop-culture subject matter, is worth the visit regardless of budget. The Azabudai Hills setting, free admission, and manageable single-room scale make it an easy stop for anyone curious how a global manga icon looks when treated with the tools of traditional Japanese printmaking.

venue.name: Shueisha Manga-Art Heritage Tokyo Gallery
venue.address_detail: Azabudai Hills Garden Plaza A, B1F
venue.about: Shueisha Manga-Art Heritage (SMAH) is a project of the publisher Shueisha dedicated to presenting manga as fine art. Since 2008 the company has been digitally archiving original manga artwork, and it now produces limited-edition fine-art prints—using archival inkjet, letterpress, collotype and other rare printing techniques—supervised by the manga artists themselves. Each edition is registered on an art blockchain network to record provenance. SMAH operates a permanent gallery in Tokyo's Azabudai Hills, opened in 2023, and has presented its artists' work at art fairs and exhibitions in Kyoto, Miami and Venice. Its program focuses on iconic Japanese manga creators, from postwar pioneers to contemporary artists, treating their original drawings as museum-grade artworks.

shows.title: ankoraci — そのまま、そのまま (Ankoraci: As It Is, As It Is)
shows.description:
Since 1992, when she first traveled to the Ainu community of Nibutani in Hokkaido, photographer Makiko Ui has spent more than three decades documenting Ainu life — not as ethnographic record but as a long, patient relationship built one visit at a time. This show pulls roughly 100 images from that archive, printed on Canon's own imagePROGRAF Pro printers, tracing her evolving closeness with individual subjects across generations.

The title comes from the Ainu phrase "ankoraci," meaning something like "leave it as it is" — a phrase that doubles as Ui's own working method. Rather than staging or explaining her subjects, she photographs people going about ordinary life: elders, ceremonies, children, landscapes, domestic scenes — letting the accumulated years of trust with her sitters register as quiet, unforced intimacy rather than spectacle.

What makes the project notable is its duration and its refusal of the exoticizing gaze that has often shaped outside photography of Ainu culture. Ui's own account describes revisiting and dismantling stereotypes she carried from childhood as she got to know specific people over three decades, and the exhibition reads less like a survey of "Ainu culture" than a record of one photographer's long, evolving relationship with specific families and communities.
shows.reception: Gallery talk Saturday, September 5, 2026, 2:00–3:00pm (no reservation needed); talk events on August 29 and September 12 require online registration

venue.name: Canon Gallery S
venue.about: Canon Gallery Ginza is one of three Canon-run photography galleries in Japan, alongside spaces in Shinagawa and Osaka. It began in 1973 as the Canon Salon on Ginza 5-chome, offering a venue and support desk for professional photographers, and was renamed Canon Gallery Ginza in 2005 when it moved to its current Ginza 3-chome location. The space runs juried, open-submission exhibitions—open to professionals and amateurs alike—on roughly two-week rotations, with many shows later touring to Canon Gallery Osaka. It also hosts several company-curated exhibitions each year and sits adjacent to the Canon Photo House Ginza.

shows.title: A Place for People — Landscapes We Live Together In (人の居場所－共に生きる風景)
shows.description:
Saiji Kanamori, a Tokyo University of the Arts-trained painter born in Nagano in 1949, has spent decades building a body of figurative oil painting around ordinary domestic and communal scenes — kitchens, gardens, gatherings of family and neighbors — rendered in a warm, slightly stylized realism that favors gentle color harmonies over drama. This exhibition, whose title translates roughly as "a place for people — landscapes we live together in," gathers new paintings that continue that long-running interest in the small, shared spaces where everyday life happens.

Kanamori made his name in the 1980s through prizes at the Shinseisaku exhibition and the Showakai exhibition, and later spent time in France as a Cultural Affairs Agency research fellow — a period that seems to have deepened his affection for scenes of quiet domesticity and human coexistence rather than pushing him toward abstraction. The paintings on view read as unpretentious records of togetherness: interiors and gardens populated by figures who seem caught mid-conversation or mid-task, treated with an illustrator's warmth and a painter's patience with light.

This is Kanamori's latest outing at the gallery that has represented him since the early 1990s, and it offers a concentrated look at an artist whose reputation rests less on formal innovation than on sustained, sincere attention to the textures of shared life.

shows.title: GROUP SHOW: 4 Artists
shows.description:
This is a well-chosen four-way conversation rather than a grab-bag group show. E'wao Kagoshima, who left Japan for New York in the 1970s and has spent decades in that city's downtown avant-garde, contributes paintings and collage-sculptures that slide between figuration and abstraction with a dreamlike, faintly unsettling wit — draftsmanship as sleight of hand. Isaac Soh Fujita Howell, also New York based and showing with the gallery for the first time, works in a darker key, painting stiff, cyborg-like figures embedded in wired, dystopian environments that owe as much to post-apocalyptic science fiction as to painting history.

Rounding out the roster are Ataru Sato and Tenki Hiramatsu, both previously familiar to the gallery's audience, whose work provides a more locally rooted counterpoint to the two New York artists. The pairing of first-time and returning artists is clearly deliberate: it lets KOSAKU KANECHIKA's Tennoz space, tucked inside the Terrada Art Complex warehouses, function as a kind of transpacific crossroads for a late-summer show.

It's a good example of how the Tennoz gallery cluster works at its best — modest in scale, specific in curatorial focus, and worth the trip out to the waterfront precisely because it isn't trying to be a blockbuster.

venue.name: KOSAKU KANECHIKA (Tennoz)
hours: Closed Sun, Mon and national holidays

shows.title: Even if I were to climb that mountain.
shows.description:
Starting on the day a rumor of imminent disaster swept across Japanese social media, Atsushi Fujimoto photographed something every single day for a full year. The resulting body of work isn't dramatic — daily life, it turns out, kept being daily life — but the accumulation of dated film frames becomes its own quiet subject: a diary made of small, largely uneventful pictures that gain weight simply by piling up.

The photographs read as a study in duration rather than incident, closer to a durational performance documented on film than to a conventional photo-essay. Fujimoto has spoken about the images functioning as a kind of shadow that keeps him company across time, tying his future self to his past one. Shown together at Totem Pole, an artist-run gallery devoted to serious photographic work, the series asks what's actually preserved when nothing in particular happens, day after day, and someone keeps pointing a camera at it anyway.

venue.name: Totem Pole Photo Gallery
venue.about: Totem Pole Photo Gallery is an artist-run photography space in Tokyo's Shinjuku ward, founded in 2008. It is operated collectively by twelve photographer-members who organize regular exhibitions of their own work alongside curated shows, events, workshops, and gallery rentals. Located on the first floor of the Dai-ni Fujikawa Building in Yotsuya, the gallery focuses on contemporary photographic practice, presenting a rotating program shaped by its member artists rather than a fixed roster of represented names outside the collective.

shows.title: Axial Tilt
shows.description:
Mariko Kitajima paints still lifes — glass vases, cut fruit, cut flowers — with a jeweler's patience, using the reflective surfaces of glass and water as a device for splitting a single subject into many contradictory versions of itself. The paintings in Axial Tilt extend that interest into a loose conceptual frame borrowed from astronomy: what would the world look like, psychologically as well as climatically, if the earth's axis were perfectly upright and nothing ever had to change?

It's a premise rather than a program, and the work doesn't illustrate it literally so much as use it to justify Kitajima's longtime subject, which is the instability of the self. Reflections warp and double the objects in front of them; light refracts unpredictably across curved glass; nothing in the compositions holds one fixed identity for long. The tilt of the title becomes a metaphor for the imperfection and constant repositioning that, in Kitajima's account, is actually what allows people to connect with each other at all.

Kitajima trained in painting at Tokyo Zokei University and has built a career on this kind of hyper-controlled, quietly uncanny realism. This is her first exhibition at AISHO's Tokyo space, presented with Osaka-based company SUNNYES, and it's a good entry point for anyone curious about the current wave of meticulous, psychologically loaded still-life painting coming out of Japan.

venue.name: AISHO
hours: Closed Sun, Mon and public holidays
venue.about: AISHO is a Japanese gallery originally established in Hong Kong in 2012 as AISHONANZUKA, later renamed AISHO Hong Kong, with a Tokyo branch opening in 2024. Founded by Aisho Miura, the gallery is rooted in street art and focuses on introducing non-academic, non-mainstream creative talents to Asian and global audiences. Its program bridges diverse cultures and explores emerging markets across East Asia. AISHO represents a wide roster of international and Japanese artists, including figures such as Hajime Sorayama, Javier Calleja, Keiichi Tanaami, and Yoon Hyup, alongside street-art-oriented artists like Cyril Kongo and Joakim Ojanen. The gallery has participated in major international art fairs including the Armory Show, Art Basel Hong Kong, Miami, and Basel, and Frieze London.

shows.title: Journeys and Life: Scenes of Horses (旅と人生、馬のいる情景)
shows.description:
Photographer Naoco Kato built this exhibition around a single animal — the horse — tracked across more than 40 countries over years of travel. The pictures on view range from quiet portraits of horses standing in foreign landscapes to wider shots of them running through open terrain, and the show doubles as something more personal: 2026 is the artist's own zodiac year of the horse, and the exhibition also marks the thirteenth anniversary of her father's death, a man who worked for Japan's central horse-racing authority.

That biographical thread gives the photographs an unusual emotional weight for what could otherwise read as a straightforward travel-photography survey. Alongside the horse pictures, Kato includes items from her father's effects and archival racetrack photographs, folding a family history into the broader visual record of horses living and working across different cultures. One image from the series was selected for the 2026 Japan Professional Photographers Society exhibition.

It's a modest, single-artist show rather than a blockbuster, but it's a good example of the kind of personal documentary photography that circulates through Ginza's smaller exhibition spaces — sincere, specific, and built from years of accumulated travel rather than a single concentrated shoot.

venue.name: Fuji Photo Gallery Ginza
hours: Last day of each show closes at 2:00pm
venue.about: Fuji Photo Gallery Ginza is an exhibition space operated by CREATE, the professional photo lab founded in 1981 (as Photo Lab Create Tokyo) that has long supported photographers and photo enthusiasts through fine printmaking. Located since 2016 in the Success Ginza First Building near Ginza and Kyobashi stations, the gallery gives professional and amateur photographers alike a place to present silver-halide (gelatin silver) prints as finished works of art. The program emphasizes the tonal depth and craftsmanship of chromogenic printing, hosting both invited and open-call ('kobo') exhibitions. The gallery operates alongside CREATE's print production and framing services, positioning itself as a bridge between photographic creation and public presentation in central Tokyo.

shows.title: Ron Mueck
shows.description:
Ron Mueck built his reputation on a simple, disorienting trick: he makes the human body at scales it was never meant to be seen at, and renders every pore, hair and vein with such patience that the illusion never quite breaks. This is his first solo show in Japan in eighteen years, and it arrives via the Fondation Cartier, which organized the exhibition before it traveled through Paris, Milan and Seoul on its way to Roppongi.

The presentation is compact but dense, with roughly a dozen sculptures spanning Mueck's career from the late 1990s to recent work, including the monumental crowd piece Mass and the very early Angel, a rare loan that doubles as a kind of origin story for everything that follows. Elsewhere, giant babies, huddled figures and other oversized or shrunken bodies turn ordinary human vulnerability into something almost geological in scale.

Alongside the sculptures, photographs and films by Gautier Deblonde pull back the curtain on Mueck's studio, showing the slow, almost obsessive process behind works that can take years to finish. It's a useful counterweight to the sculptures themselves, which are so technically dazzling that it's easy to forget a person built them by hand.

Few artists have made hyperrealism feel this emotionally loaded rather than merely technically impressive, which is why the show has been drawing steady crowds to the Mori's 53rd-floor galleries all summer.

shows.title: Picasso, through the Eyes of Paul Smith
shows.artist: Pablo Picasso; exhibition design by Paul Smith
shows.description:
This is a Picasso show designed like a fashion show — literally. The British designer Paul Smith, known for his exuberant use of stripes and color rather than for curatorial credentials, has been given free rein over roughly eighty works drawn from the Musée National Picasso-Paris, and the result is a survey of Picasso's career that looks nothing like the usual chronological march through Blue Period, Cubism and late style.

Smith's contribution is scenography rather than scholarship: rooms built around color relationships and playful juxtapositions, with paintings, ceramics and sculpture arranged the way he might arrange a shop window or a runway. It's a legitimate way of getting new eyes on very familiar material, and it works particularly well with Picasso, an artist whose restless formal experimentation always had a certain showmanship to it anyway.

For visitors who have already seen a dozen conventional Picasso retrospectives, the appeal here is less about discovering unknown masterpieces and more about watching two very different kinds of maximalist — one from early twentieth-century Málaga and Paris, one from late twentieth-century Nottingham — bounce off each other across a century of design history.

venue.name: The National Art Center, Tokyo
hours: Closed Tuesdays (closed Aug 12, open Aug 11 instead)

shows.title: Nam June Paik | The 20th Anniversary of His Passing
shows.description:
Nam June Paik effectively invented video art, and twenty years after his death, the Watari Museum is using the anniversary as an occasion to reintroduce his restless, prophetic body of work to Tokyo. The show gathers video sculptures, monitor stacks and works involving robots and closed-circuit feedback that, decades before anyone said "internet culture," were already treating television and electronic media as raw material to be cut up, looped and mocked.

Paik trained as a composer and spent time with Fluxus and John Cage before turning to television sets as sculptural objects, and that musical, anti-hierarchical sensibility runs through everything here — his monitors buzz, glitch and stack into towers with the same appetite for controlled chaos as a Cage score. Given Paik's deep, lifelong ties to Japan, where he collaborated with engineers and fellow video artists for decades, a Tokyo venue is a fitting place to revisit him.

Watari-um's small, vertical Mario Botta building has always suited object-based, immersive shows better than sprawling survey exhibitions, and a concentrated Paik presentation plays to those strengths — you move up through the floors the way you'd move through one of his own multi-monitor installations, one glowing surprise at a time.

venue.name: WATARI-UM, The Watari Museum of Contemporary Art
hours: Closed Mondays (open Jul 20, Sep 21, Oct 12, Nov 23)

shows.title: Ettore Sottsass: Design Begins Where Magic Begins
shows.description:
Ettore Sottsass spent his career arguing that furniture and objects didn't have to be quiet — they could be funny, sexy and a little absurd — and this survey at the Artizon takes that argument seriously. Best known internationally for founding the Memphis Group in 1981 and for turntables, typewriters and bookcases that look more like sculpture than product design, Sottsass gets a full career overview here, from his early ceramics and ceramics-adjacent ideas about color through to the exuberant, patterned furniture of his later decades.

The exhibition leans into his conviction that good design starts from imagination rather than function, and the installation photographs bear that out: brightly lacquered totems, room-filling shelving units and lamps that behave more like characters than fixtures, arranged less like a design-history timeline and more like a series of stage sets. It's a useful corrective for anyone who thinks of postwar Italian design purely in terms of sleek, restrained modernism.

Seeing this kind of maximalist, joy-driven design object inside the calm, art-historical rooms of the Artizon creates a productive friction of its own — Sottsass's totems and cabinets were built to disrupt exactly this kind of quiet, and here they get to do it one more time.

shows.title: Garden Next Door
shows.description:
Kei Takemura works patiently and quietly, mending broken porcelain with embroidered thread, stitching over cracks in old objects rather than hiding them, and treating the wear on everyday things as information rather than damage. That sensibility gives "Garden Next Door" its title and its logic: the show takes its cue from small, half-noticed domestic observations — a neighbor's overgrown trellis, the realization that a plant assumed to be one thing was actually another all along — and turns them into a meditation on how slowly and unevenly we actually perceive the people and places around us.

Takemura's materials are modest by design: fabric, thread, found objects, broken ceramics, the residue of everyday life reassembled into something contemplative rather than declarative. Her practice sits in a lineage of Japanese craft-based conceptualism, but her real subject is time — how memory accumulates in objects, and how presence and absence trade places when you look closely enough at something you thought you already understood.

This is the artist's first show in Taka Ishii's Roppongi space, in the same building as the gallery's other programs, and it's a good entry point for anyone curious about the quieter, more introspective side of contemporary Japanese art currently on view in a neighborhood otherwise dominated by blockbuster museum shows.

venue.name: Taka Ishii Gallery Roppongi
hours: Closed Sun, Mon and national holidays

shows.title: ARCHIVE / ACHIEVE
shows.description:
Yoshihisa Tanaka is a graphic designer whose long list of collaborators — museums, publishers, artists, paper companies — has produced posters, books, catalogues, signage and identity systems that rarely get treated as more than disposable ephemera once their job is done. This survey turns that assumption around, using the DNP Foundation's own archive alongside material held by corporations and universities to ask what actually happens to printed matter after it circulates: how it gets stored, catalogued, and eventually re-presented as a historical record of design thinking.

Rather than simply hanging finished posters and books on the wall, Tanaka has built new archival furniture for the show — storage boxes, display structures, and wrapping systems made using washi paper techniques he has researched over several years. The exhibition design itself becomes part of the argument: the humble, usually invisible apparatus of preservation (boxes, folders, mounts, plinths) is treated as a legitimate object of graphic design practice in its own right.

It's a reflective, research-driven show rather than a greatest-hits retrospective, built around Tanaka's ongoing collaborations with clients like museums and cultural institutions rather than one-off commissions. For anyone interested in the unglamorous back-end of design culture — how visual material survives, gets classified, and gets shown again — this is a rare chance to see that process made visible.

shows.title: Mujigokujo (無地極上)
shows.description:
Yosuke Urakami is a woodworker based in Togatta, a hot-spring town in Miyagi Prefecture known for its kokeshi doll craftsmen, where he settled after training for a decade in Tokyo furniture workshops. This is his fifth solo exhibition at galerie a, and it's built around a single, quietly demanding idea: objects whose whole purpose is to hold and present other objects, gaining their meaning and even their finish only once something is placed on them.

The show's title borrows a phrase from Kichinosuke Tonomura, the founding director of the Kurashiki Folk Craft Museum and a key figure in Japan's mingei (folk craft) movement — "mujigokujo," roughly "plain and supreme," referring to objects so free of applied decoration that their strength comes from form and material alone. Urakami's trays, stands, and vessels in lacquered and leafed wood pursue exactly that: pieces designed to disappear a little in service of whatever they're asked to display, whether that's a piece of jewelry, a bowl of food, or another artist's work entirely — a nod to Urakami's other life staging fashion and jewelry presentations.

Visitors can expect a tight body of new woodwork rather than a sprawling survey — precise, materially frank pieces that reward close looking at grain, joinery and surface treatment. Urakami attends the opening-day reception in person, a good opportunity to hear him talk through the ideas behind the "mujigokujo" concept directly.

venue.name: galerie a
venue.about: galerie a is a Tokyo project founded in 2020 by Nobuhiko Akiyoshi, a former buyer and wholesale agent who had worked for over a decade with domestic and international fashion designers before launching this gallery. Conceived during the COVID-19 pandemic, it operates as an online gallery that also stages physical, short-run exhibitions in Akiyoshi's own space, allowing visitors to experience works in person during limited open-gallery days. The program focuses on introducing Japan-based makers working by hand, spanning leather craft, textile sculpture, woodwork, and photography-informed leather goods, with an emphasis on artisans who pursue original, material-driven expression.

shows.title: Hernan Bas
shows.description:
Perrotin Tokyo brings back Miami-based painter Hernan Bas for a new solo show, nearly a decade after his 2018 Tokyo debut "Insects from Abroad." Bas is known for lushly detailed, expressionistic figurative paintings of androgynous young men adrift in overgrown gardens, faded interiors and other quietly decadent settings, a visual language he's built out of nineteenth-century Symbolist and Decadent literature filtered through a very contemporary sense of camp and melancholy.

His recent bodies of work have leaned into elaborate conceptual conceits — from invented naturalist expeditions to, most recently, a series of imagined portraits of fictional conceptual artists — and this Tokyo outing continues that pattern of building a whole fictional world around his recurring cast of dreamy, solitary protagonists.

Given the gap since his last Tokyo solo, this is a chance to track how Bas's dandyish, hothouse aesthetic has evolved, and to see a painter whose reputation was built in Miami and New York get a fresh reading in the compact, glass-walled Piramide space that first introduced him to Japanese audiences.

venue.name: Perrotin Tokyo
venue.about: Perrotin is an international contemporary art gallery founded in Paris in 1990 by Emmanuel Perrotin, then twenty-one years old. Over three decades the gallery has grown from a single Paris space into a network of more than twenty locations across Europe, Asia, and North America, including a gallery in Tokyo's Roppongi district. Perrotin's program is deliberately eclectic, spanning painting, sculpture, photography, and new media, and bringing together established figures, artists represented for decades, younger emerging talents, and several artist estates. The gallery describes its roster as spanning around eighteen nationalities and four continents, reflecting a stated commitment to diversity of generation, background, and medium rather than adherence to a single movement or aesthetic.

shows.title: Tennoz Contemporary
shows.description:
This four-day presentation is Tomio Koyama Gallery's contribution to Tennoz Contemporary, the art fair staged across galleries at Terrada Art Complex as the centerpiece of Tennoz Art Week 2026. Rather than a conventional solo show, it's a fair-style booth presentation devoted to the late Masahiko Kuwahara (1959–2021), whose paintings mixed pop iconography, cartoonish figures, and a wry, slightly unsettling sense of humor drawn from Japanese subculture and everyday ephemera.

Kuwahara held twelve solo exhibitions with the gallery over more than two decades, and this fair booth functions as something like a compact survey, pulling together paintings that show his loose, illustrative brushwork and recurring cast of oddball characters. It's a chance to see a substantial gallery artist's work in a condensed, fair-going format alongside neighboring booths from KAYOKOYUKI, AWASE Gallery, and Bambinart Gallery within the same space.

Because it's tied to Tennoz Art Week, the hours are unusual — a VIP evening on September 9 followed by standard fair hours September 10 through 13 — so visitors should plan around the fair's published schedule rather than the gallery's normal weekly hours.

venue.name: Tomio Koyama Gallery Tennoz
hours: Closed Sun, Mon and National Holidays
venue.about: Tomio Koyama Gallery opened in 1996 in Saga-cho, Koto-ku, Tokyo, and has since become a key platform for Japanese contemporary art. From its earliest years the gallery took part in international art fairs and served as an early point of introduction for young Japanese artists, helping shape a broader current within the country's contemporary art scene. It now operates spaces in Roppongi, Tennoz, Maebashi, and, since November 2024, Kyobashi. The program spans generations and media, representing figures such as Kishio Suga, Hiroshi Sugito, Mika Ninagawa, and Richard Tuttle alongside exhibitions of ceramic artists, reflecting an approach that moves freely across nationality and genre.

shows.title: A Tale of Blessings
shows.description:
Hiroko Toyama works in the language of Japanese Nihonga painting — mineral pigments, gold leaf, and paper — but her subject is intimate and observational rather than purely decorative. This solo debut at YUKIKOMIZUTANI centers on barn swallows, birds that migrate thousands of kilometers to nest in Japan each spring and have long been read locally as omens of prosperity and family fortune.

The show's centerpiece is "Shiki Enzu" (Barn Swallows of the Four Seasons), Toyama's most ambitious painting to date, unfolding like a handscroll through the plants and flowers of the changing seasons alongside the birds themselves. Toyama has built her practice around 'kinun,' the golden-cloud motif from classical folding screens that traditionally marks the passage of time and shifts between narrative scenes — she uses it here to stitch together a kind of visual fable about endurance, homecoming, and the dignity of small creatures living fully in the present.

It's a quiet, craft-intensive body of work rooted in a centuries-old painting tradition, and worth seeing for anyone curious how a contemporary Nihonga painter is keeping that tradition's techniques — gold leaf application, layered mineral pigment, scroll-like composition — alive with a completely current sensibility.

venue.name: YUKIKOMIZUTANI
hours: Closed Sun, Mon and National Holidays
venue.about: YUKIKOMIZUTANI is a contemporary art gallery in Tokyo, founded in 2021 with the aim of bringing contemporary art from Tokyo to an international audience. The gallery is based inside TERRADA ART COMPLEX in Tennozu, an area where the Meguro River meets Tokyo Bay, home to the largest concentration of galleries in Japan. Through its exhibition program, YUKIKOMIZUTANI supports a diverse roster of artists working across painting, sculpture, textile and installation, and takes part in major art fairs in Japan and abroad. The gallery describes its mission as elevating the role of art in contemporary culture while helping develop Tennozu Isle into a significant arts and culture hub.

shows.title: UNCONDITIONAL
shows.artist: HR Campos III, E.S.L Chen, Sean Go, Summer De Guia, Patrick De Veyra, Martin Honasan, Jing, Isadore Lerio, Nara Marin, Jason Montinola, Victoria Montinola, R.A. Tijing, Zuh Dai
shows.description:
UNCONDITIONAL gathers thirteen Filipino artists spanning several generations for a group show built around the idea of "conditions" — the forces of memory, culture, material, and everyday life that shape a work of art, and the ways artists bend those same forces into something new. It's the kind of survey exhibition that works best as an introduction: a wide cross-section of contemporary practice from Manila and beyond, rather than a single thesis pushed by one or two names.

Expect a mix of approaches — everyday materials repurposed into sculpture, familiar pop and folk motifs recontextualized, personal memory translated into something closer to myth. The connecting thread is transformation itself: works that are shaped by constraint while simultaneously escaping it. It's a useful lens for looking at contemporary Filipino art's engagement with both local history and global visual culture.

The show doubles as YOD Gallery Tennoz's contribution to Tennoz Art Week 2026, opening the same week as the neighborhood-wide Tennoz Contemporary fair, so visitors can pair it with a walk through the rest of Terrada Art Complex.

venue.name: YOD Gallery Tennoz
venue.about: YOD Gallery is a contemporary art gallery based in Osaka, with an additional space in Tokyo. Its original space in Osaka's Shinmei Building opened in 2008 and closed in 2023 after fifteen years of exhibitions. The gallery's program has featured Japanese and international artists working in sculpture, ceramics, printmaking and installation, including an annual series called "Contiguous Zone" that introduces foreign artists' work in dialogue with Japanese sensibility. Exhibiting artists have included iron sculptor Takehito Fujii and printmaker/sculptor Masashi Hattori, alongside French artists such as Agathe de Bailliencourt, Catherine Gianola and Armel Barraud. The gallery has presented both solo and group shows exploring cross-cultural exchange and material-based practice.
